---
title: "R11. Algorithmic transparency and AI"
description: "Algorithmic transparency, human oversight and using AI tools."
---

Where an algorithmic or AI tool is part of the analysis, three things follow. Publish what the tool
does. Keep a person genuinely in a position to change the outcome. Be clear about any AI used to
produce the work.

## Check whether your tool needs a transparency record

Two tests, and both have to be met. **Make the check at scoping** and record the answer either
way, because a record takes drafting and clearance.

| The test | Where NHSBSA analysis lands |
|---|---|
| **Is the organisation in scope?** | **Yes.** The standard is mandatory for arm's length bodies which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public. NHSBSA does both |
| **Is the tool in scope?** | **Usually not.** Mandatory only where the tool has a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or directly interacts with the general public. An analytical model supporting broad policy-making is deliberately outside it |

: Algorithmic transparency scope tests and where NHSBSA analysis lands

## Algorithmic transparency

The **Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS)** is how a public body publishes what an
algorithmic tool does. The record says what the tool is for and what data it was built on. It also says how
the tool affects decisions, who is accountable for it, and what oversight it has.

**First test, the organisation.** The standard is mandatory for all government departments. It is also
mandatory for arm's length bodies which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact
with the general public.[^src-atrs-section-2]

NHSBSA does both, so the organisation is in scope. It is recommended
across the rest of the public sector, which is not in mandatory scope.[^src-atrs-section-2]

**Second test, the tool.** Within an organisation in scope, the standard is mandatory for algorithmic
tools which have **a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect**. It is
also mandatory for tools which **directly interact with the general public**.[^src-atrs-section-2]

### Most of the analysis this playbook covers is outside the mandatory scope

The standard applies to tools "influencing specific operational decisions about individuals,
organisations or groups". It does not apply to "an analytical model supporting broad government
policymaking".[^src-atrs-section-2]

An eligibility rule, a risk score or a triage tool applied to individual cases is an operational
decision about individuals, so it is in scope. An analytical model that supports broad policymaking is not. **The test is what the tool decides, and about whom.** It is not
how visible the analysis is, and it is not the assurance level it scored.

Being outside the mandatory scope is not a reason to publish nothing. The Data and AI Ethics
Framework recommends publishing a record "even where a tool does not strictly fall within scope of
the ATRS".[^src-data-and-ai-ethics-framework-atrs]

Ask whether the tool is in scope in the same conversation that scores the impact. A record takes
drafting and internal clearance before it can be published, so allow time for that.

### The transparency record and Business Critical status {#transparency-and-business-critical-status}

The two decisions are separate. An analysis can be Level 4 BCA and still be out of ATRS scope. It
can be Level 2 Enhanced and in it.

Being Business Critical does not by itself put a tool in the scope of the Algorithmic Transparency
Recording Standard. Being outside that scope does not make the tool less critical. Each has its own
test, and both tests are applied at scoping.

### State in the output what the method does not show {#if-you-cannot-explain-it-say-so}

Where a method cannot be explained, **you must state that limitation in the output**. A
vendor-supplied scoring tool whose weighting is not disclosed is one example. Where the tool is in
ATRS scope, it belongs in the record as well.

Assure a model whose internal workings cannot be inspected in the same way as any other model. The
difficulty is in transparency, in having the right mix of experts available, and in understanding
what mitigations are possible. It is not a reason to assure the model less.

### Who drafts and publishes the record

The standard names two roles. An organisation in mandatory scope should have a named
**single point of contact** for the standard, whose job is to coordinate with the standard's own
team on identifying the tools in scope, drafting the records and publishing them.

If you do not know who yours is, the guidance gives
[algorithmic-transparency@dsit.gov.uk](mailto:algorithmic-transparency@dsit.gov.uk) as the
address to ask.[^src-atrs-section-2] Each record names a **senior responsible
owner**, given as a role title rather than a person. That role is ultimately accountable for the
tool in an operational context.[^src-atrs-section-6]

Who holds each of those at NHSBSA is a governance decision rather than something the standard
settles, and neither is settled yet. Until they are, the analyst drafts the record as part of
delivery. The Lead Official for Statistics clears it before publication, as for a published
statistic.

That route is this playbook filling a gap rather than the standard requiring it. Check it with the
analytical assurance mailbox in [who to ask](r3-who-to-ask.qmd).

## Meaningful human oversight

"A human is involved" is not oversight on its own. It can be true when nobody is able to change the
outcome.

**Start with the law.** UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) article 22 prohibits decisions based **solely** on automated
processing that have legal or similarly significant consequences for an individual. A service using
an algorithmic tool that affects a person's legal status or rights may use it only to **support** a
human decision-maker's decision.[^src-ai-playbook-human-oversight]

Where article 22 does not apply, how much human involvement is enough depends on three things. They
are the complexity of the output, its potential impact, and how much specialist knowledge reading it
requires.[^src-ai-playbook-human-oversight] Design, document and assess the points where human
review happens, and what further information the reviewer takes into
account.[^src-ai-playbook-human-oversight]

**Five questions make oversight real rather than nominal.**

| Question | What a usable answer looks like |
|---|---|
| **Who reviews the output?** | A named role, not "the team". Oversight with no named owner does not happen |
| **What authority do they have?** | Can they change the answer, or only note a concern about it |
| **When can they challenge or override?** | Before the decision is acted on, or only after somebody complains |
| **What gets recorded?** | That a review happened, what it considered, and what it changed |
| **Can the decision be reviewed or appealed?** | By the person it was about, and through what route |

: Questions on human oversight and what a usable answer looks like

If the reviewer has no authority to change the answer, name a reviewer who has.

## Using AI tools to do the analysis

This is different from analysis **of** an algorithmic tool. It is the everyday case: an analyst using
an AI assistant to write code, summarise a document, draft a passage or explain an error.

Using an AI tool **changes nothing about who is accountable** for the output.

- **Ask before you use a tool that is not already in use in your team.** NHSBSA has no published
  list of approved analytical AI tools, so the default is to ask rather than to assume.
- **Do not put data into a tool that is not cleared to hold it.** Patient data, personal data and
  anything under a data sharing agreement are the obvious cases. The default answer is no unless
  someone with the authority has said yes in writing.
- **Verify what comes back.** An AI output is a statistically informed guess rather than a
  fact.[^src-ai-playbook-accuracy] Code gets tested, a summary gets checked against the source, a
  figure gets recalculated.
- **Accountability does not transfer.** The analyst who signs the output owns everything in it. "The
  tool produced it" is not a finding, a caveat or a defence.
- **Record material use where it affects reproducibility.** If someone repeating your work needs to
  know a tool was used to derive something, say so in the project record, and say what was
  checked.[^src-ai-playbook-accuracy] Spell-checking a paragraph is not material. Generating the
  transformation logic behind a published figure is.
